questions.stem: A 12 year old boy is woken at 5am by severe left scrotal pain and lower abdominal pain. He has vomited three times. There was no injury. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. The left hemiscrotum is swollen and the left testis lies higher than the right with a horizontal lie. Urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain with vomiting and a high-riding, horizontally lying testis is torsion. Epididymo-orchitis is gradual with an abnormal dipstick.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: woken at 5am by severe left scrotal pain
steps.x: **Sudden** severe pain, vomiting, a **high-riding horizontal** testis and a **normal dipstick**.

elim: The pain and signs are in the scrotum; the testis itself is abnormal.
Gradual onset with dysuria or fever and a positive dipstick; his was sudden with a normal dipstick.
Usually milder, localised to the upper pole (blue dot), with a normal lie of the testis.
A varicocele is a painless or dull-aching bag of worms, not sudden severe pain with vomiting.

steps.x: **C. Testicular torsion.** Sudden pain + high horizontal testis = torsion until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy has had sudden severe right testicular pain for 2 hours, which began while he was playing a computer game. He has vomited once. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. He is too uncomfortable to stand still for long.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the scrotum?
o: Blue dot visible at the upper pole
High-riding right testis with a horizontal lie
Pain relieved by elevating the testis
Soft 'bag of worms' above the testis
questions.e: The twisted, shortened cord pulls the testis up and rotates it, giving a high-riding testis with a horizontal lie.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on examination of the scrotum?

clues: sudden severe right testicular pain for 2 hours
steps.x: Sudden severe pain with vomiting in a teenager is **torsion**: think of what a twisted cord does to the testis.

elim: Blue dot sign is torsion of the appendix testis, not of the cord.
That is a hydrocele, which is painless.
Relief on elevation favours epididymitis; in torsion pain is NOT relieved (Prehn's sign).
That is a varicocele, a dull ache rather than sudden severe pain.

steps.x: **B. High-riding right testis with a horizontal lie.** Torsion: high-riding, horizontal lie, absent cremasteric reflex.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy has a 90 minute history of sudden severe left testicular pain. Over the past 4 months he has had three short episodes of similar pain in the same testis that settled on their own within 20 minutes. He plays rugby and had mumps vaccination as a child. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which feature of his history is the most important risk factor for his current presentation?
o: Previous self-resolving episodes of testicular pain
questions.e: Previous brief self-resolving episodes suggest intermittent torsion, a recognised risk factor for full torsion.

steps.x: The question asks: which feature of his history is the most important risk factor for his current presentation?

clues: three short episodes of similar pain
settled on their own within 20 minutes
steps.x: Short episodes that untwist on their own = **intermittent torsion**.

elim: Vaccination protects against mumps orchitis; it is not a risk factor.
Torsion often occurs without trauma; rugby is not the key risk.
The side affected is not a risk factor.
Sudden onset is a feature of the presentation, not a risk factor.

steps.x: **D. Previous self-resolving episodes of testicular pain.** Previous intermittent torsion predisposes to full torsion.

questions.stem: A GP trainee reviews five male patients who each presented with acute scrotal pain over the past month. None had injury. She wants to identify the patient in whom testicular torsion was most likely, based on age and pattern of symptoms alone. Each patient is described by age and how the pain started.
questions.q: Which patient was most likely to have testicular torsion?
o: A 14 year old with pain of sudden onset
A 34 year old with pain over 3 days and dysuria
A 42 year old with a dull ache on standing
A 55 year old with a painless scrotal swelling
A 70 year old with pain after catheterisation
questions.e: Torsion peaks in adolescents and young males and starts suddenly.

steps.x: The question asks: which patient was most likely to have testicular torsion?

clues: age and pattern of symptoms alone
steps.x: Two discriminators: **age** (adolescent) and **onset** (sudden).

elim: Gradual onset with dysuria at this age suggests epididymo-orchitis.
A dull dragging ache suggests varicocele or hernia.
Painless swelling suggests hydrocele or tumour.
Infection after instrumentation is epididymo-orchitis.

steps.x: **A. A 14 year old with pain of sudden onset.** Adolescent + sudden onset = highest torsion risk.

questions.stem: An 18 year old man has had sudden right testicular pain for 3 hours. He is sexually active. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. The right testis is tender and swollen. The doctor is trying to decide between testicular torsion and epididymo-orchitis.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most support testicular torsion?
o: Negative urine dipstick for leucocytes and nitrites
Pain eased when the testis is lifted
questions.e: In torsion the urine dipstick is typically normal, without the infection markers expected in epididymo-orchitis.

steps.x: The question asks: which additional finding would most support testicular torsion?

clues: sudden right testicular pain for 3 hours
steps.x: Sexual activity tempts you towards infection, but the onset is **sudden**: look for the finding that argues against infection.

elim: Fever favours infection.
Relief on elevation favours epididymitis; in torsion it is not relieved (Prehn's sign).
The reflex is absent in torsion.
Discharge points to a sexually transmitted epididymo-orchitis.

steps.x: **B. Negative urine dipstick for leucocytes and nitrites.** Normal dipstick, absent cremasteric reflex, no relief on elevation = torsion.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man attends his GP with a small left testis. Two years ago he had left testicular torsion, presented 14 hours after the pain began, and the testis was untwisted and kept at surgery. Examination today shows a soft left testis about half the size of the right. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his examination finding?
questions.e: A testis untwisted late (beyond 6 hours) can survive but atrophy, a recognised complication of torsion.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of his examination finding?

clues: soft left testis about half the size of the right
steps.x: Late detorsion (>6 h) then a **small soft testis**.

elim: A hydrocele enlarges the scrotum and transilluminates; it does not shrink the testis.
There is no history of parotitis; the torsion history explains it.
Orchidopexy fixed the testis; recurrence gives acute pain, not a small soft testis.
A varicocele is a bag of worms; it does not cause this degree of shrinkage after torsion.

steps.x: **D. Testicular atrophy after prolonged ischaemia.** Delayed torsion: infarction, atrophy and reduced fertility.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man and his partner have been unable to conceive for 2 years. Semen analysis shows a low sperm count. At 15 he had a left orchidectomy after presenting 2 days into an episode of sudden severe testicular pain. He has no other medical history. His right testis is normal in size.
questions.q: Which is the most likely contributor to his reduced fertility?
questions.e: Late torsion leading to infarction and orchidectomy is a recognised cause of later infertility.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely contributor to his reduced fertility?

clues: 2 days into an episode of sudden severe testicular pain
steps.x: Delayed presentation, **orchidectomy** for a non-viable testis.

elim: There is nothing in the history to suggest it.
His remaining testis is normal sized; Klinefelter causes small firm testes bilaterally.
There is no history of mumps.
Nothing suggests a varicocele; the torsion history explains it.

steps.x: **D. Previous testicular torsion.** Complications of delayed torsion: infarction, atrophy, infertility.

questions.stem: A 13 year old boy is brought to the Emergency Department with 3 hours of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. He is reluctant to talk about his symptoms in front of his mother. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 120/72 mmHg. His abdomen is soft. Examination of the scrotum shows a swollen, very tender left testis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Torsion can present with abdominal pain and vomiting, and boys may be embarrassed: always examine the scrotum.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: reluctant to talk about his symptoms
steps.x: Abdominal pain and vomiting in a boy with a **tender swollen testis**.

elim: The abdomen is soft; the abnormal organ is the testis.
No diarrhoea, and there is a swollen tender testis.
Follows a viral illness with a soft abdomen but a normal scrotum.
Loin-to-groin colicky pain with haematuria; the testis is normal.

steps.x: **D. Testicular torsion.** Always examine the testes in a boy with abdominal pain.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy presents with left testicular pain. He is examined in the Emergency Department. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 122/70 mmHg. The doctor is concerned about testicular torsion and takes a focused history.
questions.q: Which feature in the history would be most typical of testicular torsion?
o: Dull ache worse at the end of the day
Pain after a kick to the groin
Pain building gradually over several days
questions.e: The signature symptom of torsion is sudden onset of severe unilateral testicular pain, often with no trauma.

steps.x: The question asks: which feature in the history would be most typical of testicular torsion?
Ask yourself what the signature symptom of torsion is.

elim: Dysuria points to epididymo-orchitis or UTI.
That is typical of a varicocele.
Torsion usually has no history of trauma.
Gradual onset favours epididymo-orchitis.

steps.x: **A. Abrupt onset of severe pain.** Torsion = sudden, severe, unilateral, often atraumatic.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy has had sudden severe right testicular pain for 1 hour. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. The right testis is high and exquisitely tender and the cremasteric reflex is absent. His father, a pharmacist, asks what is actually happening to the testis.
questions.q: Which best describes the underlying process?
o: Collection of fluid within the tunica vaginalis
Infection spreading from the urethra to the epididymis
Twisting of the spermatic cord causing testicular ischaemia
questions.e: Torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord, kinking the blood supply and causing acute ischaemia of the testis.

steps.x: The question asks: which best describes the underlying process?

clues: sudden severe right testicular pain for 1 hour
steps.x: Classic torsion: think about **the cord** and the blood supply running in it.

elim: That is a hydrocele.
That is a varicocele.
That is torsion of the appendix testis, which leaves the cord and testis normal.
That is epididymo-orchitis.

steps.x: **E. Twisting of the spermatic cord causing testicular ischaemia.** Torsion = twisted cord -> acute testicular ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy has sudden severe left testicular pain that started 9 hours ago while he was at a sleepover. He waited until morning to tell his parents. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. The left testis is high-riding and very tender. He is being prepared for theatre.
questions.q: Which is the most likely consequence of the time since onset?
o: No effect on outcome if surgery is today
Reduced chance of saving the testis
questions.e: Salvage is best within 6 hours; after that, ischaemic time sharply lowers the chance of a viable testis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely consequence of the time since onset?
More than **6 hours** of ischaemia.

elim: Delay does not affect the other side; the bilateral anatomy does.
Salvage rates fall sharply after 6 hours.
Waiting risks infarction; you cannot rely on spontaneous detorsion.
He still needs urgent exploration; a viable testis may be saved and the other side fixed.

steps.x: **C. Reduced chance of saving the testis.** The 6-hour window: salvage falls sharply after it, but still operate.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man wakes at 3am with sudden severe right scrotal pain and nausea. He has no urinary symptoms and has had one sexual partner for 5 years. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. The right testis is swollen and very tender and the cremasteric reflex is absent. Urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Torsion peaks in adolescence but also occurs in young men: sudden pain, absent cremasteric reflex and a normal dipstick.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: wakes at 3am with sudden severe right scrotal pain
steps.x: Sudden pain from sleep, absent reflex, **normal dipstick**: age 26 does not rule out torsion.

elim: Gradual, often with dysuria, fever and an abnormal dipstick.
Necrotising infection with fever, systemic toxicity and skin changes.
Usually a painless lump.
Milder pain localised to the upper pole, with a normal lie and preserved cremasteric reflex.

steps.x: **C. Testicular torsion.** Do not dismiss torsion because the patient is past adolescence.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy is seen in the Emergency Department 1 hour after the sudden onset of severe right testicular pain. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. He is pale and sweaty and is holding a sick bowl. The right side of the scrotum is swollen.
questions.q: Which additional symptom is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.e: Torsion commonly comes with nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain and unilateral scrotal swelling.

steps.x: The question asks: which additional symptom is most commonly associated with this condition?

clues: sudden onset of severe right testicular pain
steps.x: Sudden severe testicular pain and he looks nauseated.

elim: Suggests infection (epididymo-orchitis or UTI).
Suggests renal colic.
Suggests tumour or hydrocele.
Suggests a sexually transmitted infection.

steps.x: **C. Nausea and vomiting.** Torsion: pain, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, unilateral swelling.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy is seen 3 hours after sudden severe left testicular pain began, with vomiting. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. The left testis is high-riding with an absent cremasteric reflex. A scrotal ultrasound performed in the department is reported as showing normal blood flow to both testes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis and surgical exploration is the gold standard; a reassuring scan must not override strong clinical signs.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next investigation?

clues: high-riding with an absent cremasteric reflex
normal blood flow to both testes
steps.x: Classic signs **despite** a normal scan.

elim: Adds nothing and delays theatre.
Waiting risks infarction; a normal scan does not exclude torsion.
Does not distinguish torsion and delays treatment.
Helps only if infection is suspected; it cannot exclude torsion.

steps.x: **D. Surgical exploration of the scrotum.** Clinical suspicion beats imaging: explore.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has left testicular pain. It started suddenly 4 hours ago but he also says it 'stings a bit' when he passes urine. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. The left testis is tender. The doctor wants a quick bedside test to help separate torsion from epididymo-orchitis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial bedside investigation?
questions.e: A urine dipstick is typically normal in torsion, while infection markers point to epididymo-orchitis; it must not delay surgery if torsion is suspected.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial bedside investigation?
Torsion versus infection at the bedside.

elim: For sepsis, not a bedside discriminator.
Does not help distinguish these conditions.
Irrelevant to scrotal pain.
Not specific and does not separate the two.

steps.x: **E. Urine dipstick.** Normal dipstick supports torsion; never let it delay theatre.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a 10 hour history of left scrotal pain that started suddenly but has now eased considerably. He has no urinary symptoms. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Examination is equivocal: the testis is mildly tender with a normal lie. The urology registrar wants imaging.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
o: Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
questions.e: When imaging is used, scrotal Doppler ultrasound may show reduced blood flow to the testis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
Only an **equivocal** case: imaging is reasonable.

elim: Radiation, slow and does not assess testicular flow well.
Not used acutely.
Shows nothing useful about the testis.
Looks at the urinary tract, not testicular blood flow.

steps.x: **D. Scrotal Doppler ultrasound.** If imaging is used in torsion, it is Doppler ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy has 2 hours of sudden severe right testicular pain and vomiting. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. The right testis is high-riding and the cremasteric reflex is absent. The radiology department says a scrotal ultrasound can be done in 3 hours.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?
o: Discharge with analgesia and review if worse
Proceed to surgical exploration without imaging
Start antibiotics and wait for the ultrasound
Wait for the ultrasound then decide
questions.e: Torsion is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis; surgery must never be delayed for imaging.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?

clues: high-riding and the cremasteric reflex is absent
steps.x: A classic picture and a **3-hour wait**.

elim: Not used and would delay surgery.
Risks losing the testis.
Treats the wrong condition and delays theatre.
Imaging must never delay exploration when torsion is clinically suspected.

steps.x: **C. Proceed to surgical exploration without imaging.** Never wait for imaging in suspected torsion.

questions.stem: A 13 year old boy has 1 hour of sudden severe left testicular pain. His pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. The left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie, and lifting it does not ease the pain. A medical student asks what the decision to go to theatre is based on.
questions.q: On which is the diagnosis of testicular torsion mainly based before theatre?
questions.e: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis; surgical exploration then confirms it.

steps.x: The question asks: on which is the diagnosis of testicular torsion mainly based before theatre?
The signs are classic; nothing else is needed to decide on theatre.

elim: Imaging is optional and must not delay surgery.
CRP and white cells do not diagnose torsion.
For testicular cancer.
For infection; takes days.

steps.x: **A. Clinical history and examination.** Torsion: clinical diagnosis, confirmed at surgery.

questions.stem: A mother rings the out-of-hours GP service. Her 13 year old son has had sudden severe pain in his right testicle for 45 minutes and has vomited. He has no fever. He is otherwise healthy and has never had this before. She asks whether to give him paracetamol and see how he is in the morning.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Give paracetamol and review in the morning
Take him to the Emergency Department immediately
questions.e: Suspected torsion needs urgent transfer to hospital for surgical exploration; any delay risks infarction.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate advice?

clues: sudden severe pain in his right testicle for 45 minutes
see how he is in the morning
steps.x: Sudden testicular pain in a boy = **surgical emergency**.

elim: Far too slow for a surgical emergency.
Waiting risks irreversible infarction.
Imaging must not delay surgery.
This is not infection.

steps.x: **E. Take him to the Emergency Department immediately.** Suspected torsion in the community: urgent transfer to hospital.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy has emergency scrotal exploration 3 hours after the onset of left testicular pain. The left testis is twisted 720 degrees. After untwisting it turns pink and bleeds when incised. The surgeon notes that both testes hang freely within the tunica vaginalis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate surgical management?
o: Untwist now and fix both testes electively in 6 weeks
Untwist the testis and close without fixation
questions.e: A viable testis is fixed, and the other side is fixed too because the Bell-Clapper deformity is usually bilateral.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate surgical management?
Viable testis and **bilateral** free-hanging anatomy.

elim: The testis is viable; do not remove it.
The other testis has the same anatomy and is at risk.
Fixation is done at the same operation.
It may twist again.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral orchidopexy.** Viable torsion: untwist and fix BOTH sides.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy has scrotal exploration after 3 days of right testicular pain that he hid from his family. At surgery the right testis is twisted, black and does not change colour after untwisting and 15 minutes of warm packs. When incised it does not bleed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the right testis?
o: Leave it in place and review in clinic
questions.e: A non-viable, necrotic testis found at exploration is removed by orchidectomy (and the other side is fixed).

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management of the right testis?

clues: black and does not change colour
steps.x: Days of ischaemia, a black testis that does not recover.

elim: A dead testis should not be left in place.
This is infarction, not infection.
It is infarcted and should be removed.
It is already non-viable.

steps.x: **D. Orchidectomy.** Non-viable testis at exploration = orchidectomy.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy with suspected right testicular torsion has been waiting in the Emergency Department for 2 hours for an ultrasound. The pain began suddenly 3 hours ago. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. The right testis remains high-riding with an absent cremasteric reflex. The urology registrar arrives.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Arrange immediate scrotal exploration in theatre
Continue to wait for the ultrasound
questions.e: Torsion is a surgical emergency; any delay to theatre risks irreversible infarction, so imaging must not hold things up.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: waiting in the Emergency Department for 2 hours
high-riding with an absent cremasteric reflex
steps.x: The clock is running and the signs are classic.

elim: Delay risks infarction.
Even if it helps, he still needs exploration and fixation.
Never wait for imaging.
Treats infection, which this is not.

steps.x: **B. Arrange immediate scrotal exploration in theatre.** Stop waiting for scans: go to theatre.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy arrives with sudden left testicular pain that began 7 hours ago. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. The left testis is high-riding and tender with an absent cremasteric reflex. A junior doctor suggests that as he is beyond 6 hours, surgery is unlikely to help.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Salvage falls after 6 hours but some testes are still viable, and the contralateral side needs fixing: explore urgently.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?
Just past the window does not mean give up.

elim: Abandons a possibly viable testis and leaves the other side unfixed.
No role in torsion.
Imaging must not delay surgery.
He needs exploration now; the testis may still be viable.

steps.x: **E. Emergency scrotal exploration.** Beyond 6 hours: still explore as an emergency.

questions.stem: A 17 year old sexually active boy has 3 hours of sudden severe right testicular pain. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. The right testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and the pain is not relieved by elevation. Urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Doppler ultrasound and urology review in the morning
Emergency surgical exploration with bilateral orchidopexy
Oral ciprofloxacin and review in 48 hours
questions.e: Sudden pain, high horizontal testis, pain not relieved by elevation and a normal dipstick mean torsion; a slightly raised temperature and sexual activity should not lead you to antibiotics.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial management?
The distractor is the **sexual history**; the findings are torsion.

elim: Treats epididymo-orchitis; the onset and dipstick argue against it.
Imaging must not delay surgery.
Treats infection and risks losing the testis.
Not a treatment for torsion.

steps.x: **C. Emergency surgical exploration with bilateral orchidopexy.** Torsion: emergency exploration and bilateral fixation.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy is going to theatre for suspected left testicular torsion of 5 hours' duration. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 120/70 mmHg. The surgeon is consenting the boy and his mother for the operation and explains what may be done depending on what is found.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate operation to include on the consent form?
o: Exploration, bilateral orchidopexy and possible left orchidectomy
questions.e: The planned operation is exploration with bilateral orchidopexy, with orchidectomy if the testis is non-viable.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate operation to include on the consent form?

clues: suspected left testicular torsion of 5 hours' duration
steps.x: What could happen in theatre: viable or non-viable.

elim: The problem is in the scrotum.
Not the diagnosis.
The other testis also needs fixing.
That is the cancer operation, not the torsion one.

steps.x: **A. Exploration, bilateral orchidopexy and possible left orchidectomy.** Consent covers exploration, bilateral fixation and possible orchidectomy.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy has emergency surgery for right testicular torsion. At operation the surgeon finds that the tunica vaginalis is attached unusually high on the spermatic cord, so the testis hangs freely. His pulse rate before surgery was 104 bpm. The surgeon later explains the finding to a medical student.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which this anatomy predisposes to torsion?
o: It blocks lymphatic drainage of the testis
It causes a patent processus vaginalis and hernia
It compresses the testicular artery directly
The testis is not anchored and can rotate freely on the cord
questions.e: In the Bell-Clapper deformity, high investment of the tunica vaginalis lets the testis swing like a clapper inside a bell rather than being fixed.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism by which this anatomy predisposes to torsion?

clues: attached unusually high on the spermatic cord
steps.x: This is the **Bell-Clapper** deformity.

elim: Not the mechanism.
That is the mechanism of indirect inguinal hernia and hydrocele.
The anatomy permits rotation; it does not compress the artery.
The cord is not shortened by this anatomy.

steps.x: **E. The testis is not anchored and can rotate freely on the cord.** Bell-Clapper: testis swings freely, so it can twist.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy has a 2 hour history of left testicular torsion. At surgery the testis is swollen, oedematous and dusky but the surgeon can still feel arterial pulsation in the cord. After untwisting, it pinks up. A student asks why the testis was so swollen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the early swelling?
o: Congestion from occluded low-pressure venous outflow
questions.e: Twisting first occludes the low-pressure veins, causing congestion and oedema before arterial inflow is lost.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely cause of the early swelling?
Swollen but arteries still pulsating = the **veins** go first.

elim: The arterial supply was still present.
No infection; this is a vascular process.
The key early event is venous outflow obstruction.
Nothing suggests a tumour.

steps.x: **C. Congestion from occluded low-pressure venous outflow.** Torsion: veins block first -> congestion and oedema.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy had a 20 hour history of right testicular torsion. At surgery the testis is black and non-viable. The pathologist notes haemorrhagic infarction. The student on the team understands that the veins are blocked first but asks how the arterial supply is eventually lost.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of loss of arterial inflow?
o: Swelling from venous congestion overcomes the higher-pressure arterial inflow
questions.e: Venous congestion and oedema raise tissue pressure until the higher-pressure arterial inflow is compromised, causing ischaemia and infarction.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of loss of arterial inflow?

clues: how the arterial supply is eventually lost
steps.x: Follow the sequence: veins, congestion, oedema, then arteries.

elim: Not in a teenager.
Not the mechanism of torsion.
The vas does not carry the blood supply.
Not the mechanism.

steps.x: **D. Swelling from venous congestion overcomes the higher-pressure arterial inflow.** Veins -> congestion -> oedema -> arterial compromise -> infarction.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy has right testicular torsion for 2 hours. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Stroking the inner right thigh produces no elevation of the right testis, though the left testis rises normally when the left thigh is stroked.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the absent reflex on the right?
o: Compromise of the genitofemoral nerve branches within the twisted cord
Damage to the ilioinguinal nerve in the inguinal canal
questions.e: The cremasteric reflex arc (femoral branch afferent, genital branch efferent of the genitofemoral nerve) runs through the cord, so the torted cord abolishes it.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely explanation for the absent reflex on the right?

clues: produces no elevation of the right testis
steps.x: One side only: the problem is in the **cord**, not the spine.

elim: The cremasteric reflex is carried by the genitofemoral nerve.
Epididymo-orchitis usually leaves the reflex present.
The pudendal nerve is not part of this reflex.
There are no other neurological signs and the left reflex is normal.

steps.x: **A. Compromise of the genitofemoral nerve branches within the twisted cord.** Absent cremasteric reflex in torsion = genitofemoral nerve in the twisted cord.

questions.stem: A urology team audits outcomes of boys explored for testicular torsion. Every patient had the same operation, but the number of testes saved varied widely. The chart shows the time from pain onset to theatre for one boy. Visual (see item resources).

questions.q: Which factor most determines whether the testis can be saved?
questions.e: Ischaemic time is critical to viability; salvage rates fall sharply after 6 hours.

steps.x: The question asks: which factor most determines whether the testis can be saved?
